title: AgentOdyssey: Open-Ended Long-Horizon Text Game Generation for Test-Time Continual Learning Agents
claim: A single long trajectory through a generated environment shows several distinct agent abilities must work together to complete a long-horizon task.
layout: Top generation banner, then wavy trajectory timeline with annotated steps, left-to-right
description: The top row shows a robot icon with a 'Generate' arrow pointing to a highlighted 'GAME 1' card. The card gives a quest (trade with a merchant in the library) and a small location graph (Armory, Plain, Hills, Balcony, Library, Alley). Greyed-out 'GAME 2' to 'GAME N' cards follow. Below, a wavy blue trajectory runs left to right with red dots at steps 64, 257, 259, 302, 305, 311, 317 and 319. Each dot has a small location icon, a dark monospace action box (e.g. 'drop crystal ore', 'wait x6') and a light 'THINK' bubble with the agent's reasoning. Five colored labels with checkmarks mark the abilities: Skill Learning, Exploration, Episodic Memory, World Knowledge Acquisition and Long-Horizon Planning. Key words are highlighted in blue. The eye goes first to the Game 1 card, then follows the curve.
caption: Example player trajectory in an AGENTODYSSEY-generated game. AGENTODYSSEY games test five key abilities for test-time continual learning agents: exploration for finding the workbench, episodic memory for recalling the dropped trade item, world knowledge acquisition for avoiding dangerous travel times, skill learning for improving crafting via written recipes, and long-horizon planning for completing multi-step objectives such as crafting a key for trade. The trajectory shows these abilities working together over hundreds of steps to complete the quest.
abstract: For agents to learn continuously from interaction with the world at test time, they must be able to explore effectively, acquire new world knowledge and skills, retain relevant episodic experiences, and plan over long horizons. To evaluate these key abilities of test-time continual learning agents, we introduce AgentOdyssey, a novel evaluation framework that procedurally generates open-ended text games with rich entities, world dynamics, and long-horizon tasks. Critically, AgentOdyssey goes beyond the conventional machine learning assumption that learning does not occur at test time by placing agents in a continuous, long-horizon setting that interleaves learning and inference throughout deployment. We further propose a multifaceted evaluation methodology that measures not only game progress but also offers diagnostic tests on world knowledge acquisition, episodic memory, object and action exploration, action diversity, and model cost. We evaluate diverse agent paradigms across six generated games. Our experimental results reveal critical limits in agents' key abilities, as well as factors that influence their meaningful horizon. Although performance scales with stronger base models, even the top agent remains far below human performance on a demanding long-horizon game, leaving substantial headroom for improvement. Additionally, a focused study of agent test-time training finds that, although short-term memory is beneficial, agents trained with supervised fine-tuning still suffer from catastrophic forgetting, suggesting that parametric continual learning for agents remains an open challenge.
